title: Iterators
intro: An iterator hands out items one at a time, and does nothing until something asks for them. You chain steps like `filter`, `map`, `zip` and `fold` onto it instead of writing the loop. The only surprise is how many `&` the closure receives.

coming_from.go: Go's standard library has no `map` or `filter` for slices, so this replaces a hand-written loop. The chain is lazy: nothing runs until `.collect()` or `.sum()`, and the closure often gets a reference, like `&i32`, instead of the number.
coming_from.kotlin: This is Kotlin's `filter` and `map`, but lazy like a `Sequence`: you start with `.iter()` and finish with `.collect()`. There is no `it`, and the closure gets references, so `filter` sees `&&i32`.
coming_from.python: A chain like `.iter().filter(...).map(...)` is lazy like a generator expression, and `.collect()` is `list(...)`. The surprise is that closures get references, so you write `|&&n|` or `**n` to reach the number.
coming_from.typescript: Array `filter` and `map` build a new array at each step, but a Rust chain is lazy until `.collect()` or `.sum()`. You start with `.iter()`, and the closure gets references (`&&i32` in `filter`) instead of plain numbers.
coming_from.java: `iter().filter().map().collect()` is a Stream pipeline ending in `toList()`, and it's just as lazy. The catch is that items are references, so `filter` gets `&&i32` and you peel them off with patterns like `|&&n|`.
coming_from.csharp: `filter` is `Where` and `map` is `Select`, lazy like LINQ, and `collect()` is the `ToList()` at the end that runs the whole chain. The catch is that `.iter()` yields references, so `filter` gets `&&i32` and you write `|&&n|` or `**n` to get the number.
coming_from.c: C has no closures or iterator chains, so you'd write one loop that tests and stores. Rust's chain compiles down to much the same loop; the cost is getting used to closures that receive references like `&&i32`.
coming_from.cpp: `filter` and `map` are `std::views::filter` and `std::views::transform`, lazy in the same way, and `collect()` is C++23's `std::ranges::to`. A C++ lambda taking `auto n` gets a copy of each int; Rust's `filter` lends you a reference to the item instead, so you write `|&&n|` to get the number.

notes: Why `&&`? `.iter()` lends you each item, so it is `&i32`. `filter` has to look at the item and then still pass it on, so it can't hand it over. It lends it to your closure again. A lend of a lend is `&&i32`.
`map` takes the item and returns something new, so it gets the item as-is (`&i32` here). Rule: `filter`, `find`, `take_while` get one extra `&`. `map`, `for_each`, `fold` don't.
`|&&n|` is a pattern that strips both `&` and gives you the plain number. The toolkit below explains references in iterators properly, and how to avoid them with `.copied()` or `.into_iter()`.
Chains are lazy. Nothing runs until `collect()` or `sum()`. In a release build they typically compile to the same code as a hand-written loop.

gotcha.title: Doing arithmetic on what `filter` hands you
gotcha.looks_fine: In Kotlin, `it` inside `filter` is the element itself. You never think about references.
gotcha.rust_sees: Here `n` is `&&i32`, a reference to a reference to a number. `%` works on a number or on one reference to a number, but not through two.
gotcha.why: Method calls like `n.abs()` follow references automatically, any number of them. Arithmetic follows one `&`, and comparisons want the same type on both sides. So this only bites in closures that do arithmetic or comparisons on a `&&`. The toolkit below explains where the second `&` comes from, and how to avoid it.

go.says: Go has no `filter` in its standard library. You would write a loop, where `n` is just the number.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints [2, 4, 6]. `n` is the number itself, so `n % 2` works with no references to follow.

python.says: Python prints [2, 4, 6]. `n` is the number itself, so `n % 2` works with no references to follow.
python.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
evens = list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums))
print(evens)

typescript.says: Prints [ 2, 4, 6 ]. In TypeScript `n` is the number itself, so `n % 2` works as written.

java.says: This prints [2, 4, 6]. Java unboxes the Integer for `%` automatically, so there are no layers of references to think about.

csharp.says: LINQ lambdas get the item itself, so `n % 2` works and prints [2, 4, 6]. Rust's `filter` hands you a reference to a reference, which is why the same line fails there.

c.says: C has no closures or iterator chains. The C version is a plain loop over `nums[i]`, so this mix-up of `&&i32` and `i32` cannot happen.

cpp.says: The lambda takes `auto n`, a copy of each int, so `n % 2` works and this prints `2 4 6`. Rust's `filter` lends the item instead of copying it, so the closure gets `&&i32` and you take the `&`s off yourself.

python.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

evens_squared = [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
total = sum(nums)
print(f"{evens_squared} {total}")
